title: The impacts of nature experience on human cognitive function and mental health
review_question: To review and synthesize the effects of nature experience on human cognitive function and mental health, drawing from environmental psychology, urban planning, medical literature, and landscape aesthetics.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Studies using traditional psychology tests, surveys, and questionnaires to quantify impacts on attention, concentration, memory, impulse inhibition, stress, and mood. Focused on positive effects. Employed a 'snowball' method, starting with foundational work by Stephen and Rachel Kaplan and Roger Ulrich.

synthesis_conclusions: Nature experience positively impacts human cognitive function (memory, attention, concentration, impulse inhibition) and mental health (mood, stress).
These benefits are supported by a strong foundation of research across environmental psychology, urban planning, medicine, and landscape aesthetics.
Both unconscious (Stress Reduction Theory, Attention Restoration Theory) and conscious (preferences, connection to nature) mechanisms contribute to these benefits.
Exposure to nature, whether through images, window views, or physical presence, yields psychological benefits.
Short durations of 'green exercise' (e.g., 5 minutes) can yield significant mental health benefits, particularly for self-esteem and mood.
The benefits of nature experience can be conceptualized as a 'psychological ecosystem service'.
evidence_gaps: Further inquiry into specific elements of the natural environment that impact cognitive function and mental health.
Determining the most effective type, duration, and frequency of contact with nature.
Identifying the possible neural mechanisms responsible for the documented effects (e.g., using fMRI).
Developing formal, quantifiable, and consistent metrics to compare 'urban' and 'natural' environments.
More extensive work covering the full range of variety, duration, frequency, and spatial scale of nature exposure.
Systematically incorporating the repercussions of opinions about nature on individual psychological benefits.
Examining more detailed behavioral effects using modern psychology tests (e.g., filtering tasks, complex operation span tasks, distraction tests).
Assessing the persistence of measured impacts once subjects return to normal environments.
Understanding if biodiversity independently corresponds to psychological benefits.
Exploring whether changes in context itself (novelty) plays a role in observed stress reductions, unrelated to natural elements.

moderators.effect: Individuals dealing with greater crisis/stress experienced greater stress relief from nature.
More mentally fatigued subjects were more likely to choose a restorative walk in a natural environment.
Both men and women showed improved self-esteem, but only men showed significant mood improvement.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Men: improved mood and self-esteem. Women: improved self-esteem.

moderators.effect: Greatest benefit for mood and self-esteem from 5 minutes of activity, followed by an entire day; lowest from 10 minutes to half-day doses.
moderators.subgroup_effects: 5 minutes: highest benefit. 10 min - half-day: lowest benefit. Full day: high benefit.

limitations: Existing literature often uses loose and vague descriptions of 'urban' and 'natural' environments.
A large percentage of studies have been conducted within a small range of landscape types and similar durations/frequencies of nature exposure.
The review focuses on positive effects, with few investigations of potential negative effects of nature experience.
Causal mechanisms for nature's impact on mental and physical state are controversial and require further research.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Scholars spanning a variety of disciplines have studied the ways in which contact with natural environments may impact human well‐being. We review the effects of such nature experience on human cognitive function and mental health, synthesizing work from environmental psychology, urban planning, the medical literature, and landscape aesthetics. We provide an overview of the prevailing explanatory theories of these effects, the ways in which exposure to nature has been considered, and the role that individuals’ preferences for nature may play in the impact of the environment on psychological functioning. Drawing from the highly productive but disparate programs of research in this area, we conclude by proposing a system of categorization for different types of nature experience. We also outline key questions for future work, including further inquiry into which elements of the natural environment may have impacts on cognitive function and mental health; what the most effective type, duration, and frequency of contact may be; and what the possible neural mechanisms are that could be responsible for the documented effects.
